vignette:
Mr. Thao's Careful Routine

Mr. Thao is a lean, quiet man of seventy-six who has worked in the same warehouse for the past eighteen years. He arrives every morning at 5:45 a.m., before anyone else, and spends his first hour organizing the receiving area with meticulous precision. His coworkers know him as reliable and steady-the kind of man you can count on to notice if a shipment is missing a box or if the loading dock door doesn't close properly. What they don't see is the reason he comes so early: he needs time alone to walk the perimeter, to check the exits, to ensure the space is secure before others arrive.

Mr. Thao was forty-two years old when he fled his country during the war. He had been a merchant then, selling textiles in a busy market, and he had a wife and two young children. One afternoon in 1989, soldiers came through the market. There was shouting, then gunfire. Mr. Thao ran. He doesn't speak much about what happened next-only that his family was separated in the chaos, and he was eventually able to escape on a boat. He never saw them again.

He spent three years in a refugee camp before being resettled in America. He learned English slowly, working various jobs until he found the warehouse work. It was simple, physical, and importantly, it was his to control. He could manage the space, understand its rhythms, predict what would happen next.

For decades, Mr. Thao functioned well enough. He had built a modest life-a small apartment, regular routines, a few acquaintances from work. But in the last year, something has shifted. He tells me that loud noises now make him jump in ways that feel involuntary and embarrassing. The sound of a truck backing up, the beeping of the loading equipment, even a car backfiring outside his apartment-these sounds send a surge of adrenaline through his body that takes hours to settle. His heart races. His hands shake.

He has also begun having trouble sleeping. He goes to bed around nine o'clock but lies awake until midnight or later, his mind cycling through the same memories. When he does sleep, he sometimes wakes up gasping, unsure where he is. On these nights, he gets up and walks around his apartment, turning on lights, checking locks. He has added three new deadbolts to his door in the past six months.

At work, Mr. Thao finds himself becoming irritable with younger employees in ways that surprise him. When someone moves a box he has organized or doesn't follow the system he has established, he feels a flash of anger that seems disproportionate to the situation. He recognizes this isn't entirely fair, but he struggles to control it. He has started eating lunch alone in his car rather than in the break room, finding the unpredictability of casual conversation exhausting.

Most troubling to Mr. Thao is that he has begun avoiding certain parts of the warehouse-the back corner near the storage cages where visibility is limited, and the upper mezzanine where there is only one exit. He has worked around these spaces for nearly two decades, but now they feel unsafe in a way he cannot fully explain. His supervisor has noticed he is taking longer routes to complete tasks, and Mr. Thao has made vague excuses about his aging knees.

He describes feeling perpetually on edge, as though something bad is about to happen. This sense of impending danger follows him from the warehouse to his apartment, coloring his interactions and his quiet hours alone. He is not sure how much longer he can continue this way.
